papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Results (density QNN framework, preparation, gradient extraction, Proposition 1 and Corollary 1, overfitting section), Discussion. Supplementary proofs and most numerical-result sections not read in full.
papers.what_it_is: A theory-plus-numerics paper that introduces density quantum neural networks (mixtures of trainable unitaries) and analyzes their expressivity and gradient cost.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Hastings-Campbell Mixing lemma converts benefits from linear combination of unitaries models into density models with similar performance guarantees but shallower circuits, and that they prove this under certain assumptions.
assertions.anchor: Abstract; Results, Preparing density quantum neural networks, p.3
quotes: For expressivity, the Hastings-Campbell Mixing lemma converts benefits from linear combination of unitaries into density models with similar performance guarantees but shallower circuits.
We prove this, under certain assumptions, using the Hastings-Campbell Mixing lemma from randomised quantum circuit compiling.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the result is proved under assumptions; the theorem and its assumptions were not read in the supplement, so no higher grade is suggested.
assertions.reader_inference: The performance guarantee depends on assumptions not examined here.

assertions.value: The paper states that when no parameters are shared across sub-unitaries, the density model introduces an O(K) overhead for gradient extraction, and that if K = O(log(N )) and each sub-unitary admits a backpropagation scaling, the density model will also admit a backpropagation scaling.
assertions.anchor: Corollary 1 and Figure 2 caption, p.4-5 (proof in Supp. Mat. B.1)
quotes: As a result, the full model introduces an O(K) overhead for gradient extraction.
If K = O(log(N )) and each sub-unitary admits a backpropagation scaling for gradient extraction, the density model will also admit a backpropagation scaling.
assertions.certainty_reason: Corollary 1 and Proposition 1, p.4, proof in Supp. Mat. B.1 (proof not read; the text says it follows from linearity of the model).

assertions.value: The authors report that, for a budget of N parameters, distributing them across a density QNN with shallow sub-unitaries gave better results from the perspective of overfitting than increasing the circuit depth of a single data reuploading classifier, on data generated by Chebyshev polynomials.
assertions.anchor: Results, overfitting and data reuploading, p.8-9
quotes: In summary, we find that given a budget of N parameters, distributing these across a density QNN with shallow sub-unitaries will lead to better results (from the perspective of overfitting) than increasing the circuit depth of a single quantum classifier.
assertions.certainty_reason: One empirical study on synthetic single-qubit data.
assertions.reader_inference: The test is a single-qubit synthetic example, so it does not show overfitting mitigation on real data.

assertions.value: The authors state that in this work the sub-unitary circuit structures are fixed once chosen, trainability comes only from the sub-unitary parameters and the coefficients, and variable-structure circuits such as those from quantum architecture search are not incorporated.
assertions.anchor: Results, Density quantum neural networks, p.2
quotes: In this work, we assume that the sub-unitary circuit structures, once chosen, are fixed, and the only trainability arises from the parameters
we do not incorporate variable structure circuits learned for example via quantum architecture search.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of scope, Results p.2.

papers.title_in_file: Paving the Way to Hybrid Quantum-Classical Scientific Workflows
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Related Work (skimmed), Section 5.3 start, Section 6.2-6.3, Conclusion. Sections 3, 4, 5.1-5.2 and 7 not read in full.
papers.what_it_is: A conceptual and architectural paper on turning classical scientific workflows into hybrid quantum-classical workflows, illustrated with a molecular dynamics use case.

assertions.value: The authors state that, starting from a molecular dynamics use case, they describe a possible architecture for a hybrid workflow management system that identifies software components to integrate classic and quantum architectures.
quotes: Based on this analysis, we describe a possible architecture for a hybrid WMS, identifying software components that would facilitate the integration of classic and quantum architectures.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of what it delivers, Section 8.
assertions.reader_inference: The contribution is a design proposal; no quantum speedup or run on quantum hardware is reported in the parts read.

assertions.value: The authors state that their approach assumes a label for each classic task that maps it to its quantum counterpart, so it depends on the source code corpus used to train the classification model.
quotes: Another issue is related to the code classification-based approach since we assume that there is a label for each classic task that allows us to map it to its quantum counterpart.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 6.3 lists it as a limitation.

assertions.value: The authors state that circuit synthesis and mapping in the proposed system focus on the quantum circuit model, and that photonic machines, while able to execute each circuit, performed best with the measurement-based model, so the mapping might not guarantee the best performance there.
quotes: While each circuit can be also executed on photonics hardware, these machines proved to have the best performance with measurementbased model [94], therefore circuit synthesis and mapping might not guarantee the best performance.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 6.3 lists it as a limitation.

papers.title_in_file: Exploring Quantum Machine Learning for Weather Forecasting
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Methods (dataset and model overview), text of Results for temperature and wind, Conclusion. Tables and figures not read as images.
papers.what_it_is: A simulation study comparing six QNN configurations with a classical RNN for temperature and wind speed forecasting at one Brazilian city.

assertions.value: The authors report that a QNN reached 69.6% accuracy for temperature prediction and that a three-layer EntanglingLayer QNN reached 84.4% accuracy for wind speed forecasting.
quotes: QNN achieved 69.6% accuracy for temperature prediction, while a three-layer EntanglingLayer QNN reached 84.4% accuracy for wind speed forecasting.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study on one site and one year of data.

assertions.value: The authors report that the best temperature result was QNN Experiment 2 with a single variational layer at a MAE of 0.304, and that the RNN MAE of 0.347 was intermediate, outperforming half of the QNN simulations.
assertions.anchor: Section III A, temperature results, p.6-7
quotes: The best result in this section corresponds to QNN Experiment 2 with a single variational layer, achieving a MAE of 0.304.
As previously discussed, the MAE of 0.347 achieved by the RNN was intermediate, outperforming half of the QNN simulations.
assertions.certainty_reason: Mean over 10 runs of one study; test set is a short window.
assertions.reader_inference: Half of the QNN configurations were worse than the RNN, so the QNN advantage depends on the chosen configuration.

assertions.value: The authors state that the analysis covers the Brazilian city of Barreiras with one year of data from May 1st, 2023, to April 30th, 2024, split into 96.2% training and 3.8% testing, and that the quantum results were obtained on the KUATOMU quantum simulator.
assertions.anchor: Section II A; Section III A; Acknowledgements, p.3-4, 14
quotes: The analyzed region was the Brazilian city of Barreiras, located in the state of Bahia.
Considering the dataset spans one year (from May 1st, 2023, to April 30th, 2024), the data were partitioned into training and testing subsets corresponding to 96.2% and 3.8%, respectively.
for access to the KUATOMU quantum simulator, which was used in obtaining results.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its setup, Sections II A, III A and Acknowledgements.
assertions.reader_inference: A single location, one year and a simulator limit how far the result generalizes.

assertions.value: The authors state that the limitations of the NASA POWER dataset, including its daily resolution and non-geostationary satellite sources, may impact forecasting precision.
quotes: The limitations of the NASA POWER dataset, including its daily resolution and non-geostationary satellite sources, may also impact
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own stated limitation, Conclusion p.14.

papers.title_in_file: Graph Algorithms with Neutral Atom Quantum Processors
papers.version_note: arXiv 2403.11931v1, 18 Mar 2024. Authors are at PASQAL, a neutral atom hardware vendor.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Section 3 (UD-MIS passage), Section 4.2 limitations, Box on repetition rate, Section 6 Conclusion. Other sections skimmed only.
papers.what_it_is: A review by a neutral atom hardware company of graph algorithms and embedding techniques on neutral atom QPUs, with hardware outlook.

assertions.value: The authors state that the paper reviews advancements in quantum algorithms for graph problems on neutral atom QPUs and discusses recently introduced embedding and problem-solving techniques.
quotes: In this paper, we review the advancements in quantum algorithms for graph problems running on neutral atom Quantum Processing Units (QPUs), and discuss recently introduced embedding and problem-solving techniques.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of scope, Abstract.
assertions.reader_inference: The authors work at a vendor of neutral atom hardware, so the positive outlook is a vendor perspective.

assertions.value: The authors state that the full processing cycle reduces the repetition rate of the useful computation to few Hz, and that the effective rate is reduced further by the finite probability of assembling a defect-free register.
quotes: reduces the repetition rate of the useful computation to few Hz.
In addition, the effective repetition rate is even scaled down by the finite probability of assembling a defect-free quantum register at each cycle.
assertions.certainty_reason: A limitation the authors state about current neutral atom devices (Box 4); no measurement is given in the text read.

assertions.value: The authors state that combining the listed hardware techniques should raise the effective repetition rate to the 100 Hz or kHz range.
quotes: Overall, the combination of all those techniques should raise the effective repetition rate to the 100 Hz or kHz range.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor-affiliated projection about its own technology; no demonstration in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors report, citing prior work, that for long enough evolution times experimenters identified a quadratic quantum speedup with respect to classical simulated annealing on hard graphs, and that the locality of UD-MIS makes it relatively easy to approximate classically.
quotes: For long enough evolution times, the authors experimentally identified a quadratic quantum speedup with respect to classical simulated annealing on hard graphs.
Intriguingly, the locality of UD-MIS makes it relatively easy to approximate classically, and there even exists a so-called polynomial-time approximation scheme
assertions.certainty_reason: Results the paper attributes to other work (its Refs. 36 and 41).

papers.title_in_file: Variational Quantum Algorithms in the era of Early Fault Tolerance
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Background 2.1, Methodology 5 (opening), Evaluation 6.1-6.2, Discussion, Conclusion start. Architecture sections 3-4 not read in full.
papers.what_it_is: A simulation study of variational quantum algorithms under partial quantum error correction (pQEC) in an early fault-tolerance regime.

assertions.value: The authors report that pQEC outperforms NISQ execution by 9.27x on average and up to 257.54x, even for VQA ansatz explicitly tailored for the NISQ regime.
quotes: Our results show that this strategy for VQA outperforms NISQ execution by 9.27x on average and up to 257.54x, even for VQA ansatz explicitly tailored for the NISQ regime.
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation result from one study under assumed error rates.
assertions.reader_inference: The ratio is against a modeled NISQ baseline, not a hardware run.

assertions.value: The authors state that they use density matrix simulations for 8 and 12 qubits and Clifford state simulations for larger numbers of qubits.
quotes: As discussed in Section 5.2, we use density matrix simulations for 8, and 12 qubits and Clifford state simulations for larger number of qubits.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its evaluation setup, Section 6.1.

assertions.value: The authors report that in small-scale density matrix simulations of Ising, Heisenberg, H2O, H6 and LiH Hamiltonians, pQEC consistently outperforms NISQ.
quotes: We observe the pQEC consistently outperforms NISQ.
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation result from one study; per-Hamiltonian ratios are in the text but include symbols not copied.

assertions.value: The authors state that implementing and evaluating the NISQ-era error mitigation techniques in the EFT context is beyond the scope of this work.
quotes: Implementing and evaluating all of these techniques in the EFT context is beyond the scope of this work.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own stated scope limit, Section 7.

papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Section 4 complexity discussion, Section 5 methodology, annealing-time and time results text, Conclusion. Section 3 and tables not read in full.
papers.what_it_is: A paper that formulates SVM training as a QUBO, runs it on a D-Wave Advantage annealer, and compares accuracy and runtime with Scikit-learn.

assertions.value: The paper states that if the precision for all parameters is fixed, the qubit footprint and time complexity of the quantum approach would be O(N 2), which it calls an order of magnitude better than the classical algorithm at O(N 3), and that estimating ST99 and ST99(OPT) for a generic QUBO formulation of the SVM problem is beyond the scope of the present work.
quotes: The resulting qubit footprint would be O(N 2), and time complexity would also be be O(N 2). This time complexity is an order of magnitude better than the classical algorithm (O(N 3)).
Estimating ST99 and ST99(OPT) for generic QUBO formulation of the SVM problem is beyond the scope of the present work.
assertions.certainty_reason: An argued complexity under stated assumptions (fixed precision, constant annealing time and repetitions); the annealing time is not bounded.
assertions.reader_inference: The O(N 2) figure treats annealing time as constant, which the paper itself says is only observed in practice for small problems.

assertions.value: The authors report that the quantum approach obtains accuracies on par with the classical Scikit-learn approach across five benchmark datasets.
quotes: We show that our quantum approach obtains accuracies on par with the classical approach.
Our training results demonstrate that the quantum approach's accuracy is comparable with the classical approach.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study on small benchmark datasets.
assertions.reader_inference: The annealing-time test in the same paper found Scikit-learn consistently better, so 'on par' is not uniform.

assertions.value: The authors report that when training with a dataset with 8 million features, the quantum annealer outperforms the classical computer by achieving up to 4.48 times faster computation, and they note that the Scikit-learn algorithm may not be the most efficient classical algorithm.
quotes: When training with a dataset with 8 million features, the quantum annealer outperforms the classical computer by achieving up to 4.48

While the Scikit-learn's algorithm for training SVMs may not be the most efficient classical algorithm, it certainly is one of the most widely used algorithms in the literature and runs in O(N 3) time.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result on synthetic data from one study; baseline is one widely used classical implementation.
assertions.reader_inference: The baseline is not the best classical SVM solver, so the speedup is not against state of the art; the authors say so themselves.

assertions.value: The authors report that as annealing time increased, the Scikit-learn model consistently performed better and had less variance in accuracy than the quantum and simulated annealing models, with no statistically significant accuracy difference from longer annealing.
quotes: Even as the annealing time increased, the Scikit-learn model consistently performed better and consisted less variance in accuracy than the quantum and simulated annealing models.
There wasn't a statistically significant difference in the accuracy by increasing the annealing time as the mean accuracies of each test were within one standard deviation of each other.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study, 10 repetitions per condition.

papers.title_in_file: Optimizing Low-Energy Carbon IIoT Systems with Quantum Algorithms: Performance Evaluation and Noise Robustness
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Methodology (skimmed), noise-model analysis text, Discussion and Conclusion. Tables and algorithm listings not read in detail.
papers.what_it_is: A simulation study applying three QNN variants (Pennylane, Qiskit, hybrid) to two small IoT datasets with a noise-model robustness analysis.

assertions.value: The authors report that for the RODD dataset QNNP achieved the highest accuracy at 0.95, followed by QNN-H at 0.91 and QNN-Q at 0.80, and that for the GPSD dataset QNN-P attained 0.94, QNN-H 0.87 and QNNQ 0.74.
quotes: For the RODD dataset, QNNP achieved the highest accuracy at 0.95, followed by QNN-H at 0.91 and QNN-Q at 0.80.
Similarly, for the GPSD dataset, QNN-P attained an accuracy of 0.94, QNN-H 0.87, and QNNQ 0.74.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study on two datasets.

assertions.value: The authors state that QNN-P was chosen as the most promising candidate for a detailed noise analysis, and report that the depolarizing and amplitude damping models exhibited superior resilience while the bit flip, phase flip and bit phase flip models were highly sensitive to noise.
assertions.anchor: Section III, noise analysis summary, p.9
quotes: This made QNN-P the most promising candidate for a detailed noise analysis.
For both datasets, the depolarizing and amplitude damping models exhibited superior resilience.
In contrast, the bit flip, phase flip, and bit phase flip models were highly sensitive to noise, with significant drops in accuracy even at low noise levels.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The abstract says the models' robustness was verified, but the detailed noise analysis covered QNN-P only.

assertions.value: The authors state that the superiority of the algorithms is demonstrated through simulation experiments on two low-energy carbon datasets, and that the complexity and runtime metrics in their tables are calculated for 300 data points.
assertions.anchor: Section I contributions; Section IV Discussion, p.2, 10
quotes: The superiority of these algorithms is demonstrated through extensive simulation experiments on two lowenergy carbon datasets, with their performances compared using key evaluation metrics.
These metrics are calculated for 300 data points.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its experimental setup, Sections I and IV.
assertions.reader_inference: Results come from simulation on small datasets, not from quantum hardware.

assertions.value: The authors state that deploying quantum solutions in real-world IoT systems faces challenges like hardware limitations, high costs, and infrastructure needs, including stable environments and access to QPUs.
assertions.anchor: Section IV Discussion and Conclusion, p.10
quotes: Deploying quantum solutions in real-world IoT systems faces challenges like hardware limitations, high costs, and infrastructure needs, including stable environments and access to QPUs.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own stated limitation, Section IV.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum One-class Classification With a Distance-based Classifier
papers.version_note: arXiv 2007.16200v2, 6 May 2021 (file is in the 2020 folder)
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Conclusion, and the experiment-setup text. Sections II-IV and the results tables were skimmed; two-column layout interleaves some table text.
papers.what_it_is: A paper proposing a minimal Quantum One-Class Classifier derived from the Hadamard Classifier, tested in simulation and on two IBM devices.

assertions.value: The authors report that in the error-free experiment QOCC accuracy is equivalent to HC accuracy, and that QOCC has equivalent or better accuracy in real quantum devices.
assertions.anchor: Section I Introduction, p.1-2; Section VII Conclusion, p.8
quotes: In the error-free experiment, results show that QOCC accuracy is equivalent to HC accuracy.
QOCC has equivalent or better accuracy in real quantum devices.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study on small datasets and two devices.
assertions.reader_inference: Per-dataset device accuracies in the tables vary and some are lower than simulation; the summary claim was not checked row by row.

assertions.value: The authors state that QOCC removes the class and index quantum registers of HC, and that HC needs a 2-qubit measurement to classify while QOCC requires only a one-qubit measurement.
quotes: We reduced HC by removing its class and index quantum registers maintaining accuracy.
Besides that, HC needs a 2-qubit measurement to perform the classification, and QOCC requires only a onequbit measurement.
assertions.certainty_reason: A design property of the proposed circuit, stated in the Introduction and Section V.

assertions.value: The authors state that experiments ran first in an error-free simulation environment and then on two non-error-corrected quantum processors, ibmq athens and ibmq santiago.
quotes: and then in two non-error-corrected quantum processors ibmq athens and ibmq santiago.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its experimental setup, Section I.

assertions.value: The authors state that using QOCC on multiclass datasets and inserting trainable parameters to improve its accuracy are future work.
quotes: Possible future works are to investigate how to use the QOCC to classify multiclass datasets and explore how to insert parameters into the classifier to improve its accuracy.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own stated limit of the work, Section VII.
